In many countries today, people wait until they are older before they have children. For example, many couples now have their first baby in their thirties instead of their twenties. In my opinion, this is generally a positive development.

The main reason is that older parents are usually more ready for the responsibility. When people are in their thirties, they have normally finished their education and have a stable job, so they have more money to take care of a child. They can pay for good food, clothes and education, and they does not need to depend on their own parents. In contrast, young couples often have financial problem and this can cause stress in the family.

Another reason is that older parents are more mature. They have more experience of life, and they already did many things they wanted to do, like travelling or building a career. Because of this, they are more patient and they can give more time and attention to their children. They also know better what kind of values they want to teach them.

However, having children later has some disadvantages. It can be more difficult for women to become pregnant when they are older, and parents may have less energy to play with young children. In addition, children may have less time with their grandparents, because the grandparents are also very old.

In conclusion, even though there are some problems, I believe having children later in life is a positive development. Parents who is older are usually more stable in money and more mature, and this is good for the children's future.

samples.text:
Across much of the world, the average age at which people become parents has been rising steadily. While there are understandable reasons for this, I believe that the trend is, on the whole, a negative development, both for families and for society.

It is true that delaying parenthood has some advantages. People who have children in their thirties or forties are often more financially secure and emotionally mature than younger parents. They may also have had time to complete their education and establish a career, which can reduce stress within the family.

However, there are significant biological disadvantages. It is widely recognised that fertility declines with age, so couples who wait may find it difficult to conceive and may need expensive medical treatment, which does not always succeed. As a result, some people who wanted children end up having fewer than they hoped, or none at all. Moreover, older parents may have less energy for the physical demands of raising young children.

The trend also has consequences across generations. When each generation has children later, grandparents are older when their grandchildren are born and may be less able to help with childcare or to enjoy an active role in their lives. At the same time, parents may find themselves caring for young children and elderly relatives simultaneously, which put considerable pressure on them. At a national level, later parenthood tends to contribute to lower birth rates, which creates an ageing population and places a heavier burden on the working-age population.

In conclusion, although older parents often enjoy greater stability, the difficulties with fertility, the strain on families and the long-term demographic effects make this trend largely negative. Governments could reduce it by offering better support to younger parents, such as affordable housing and childcare.

samples.text:
In many countries, the age at which people have their first child has risen considerably over the last few decades, as longer education, demanding careers and high housing costs encourage couples to postpone parenthood. Although this shift carries genuine risks, I believe it is, on balance, a positive development.

The principal benefit is that children are more likely to be born into stable circumstances. Parents who have completed their studies and established themselves professionally are generally better placed to provide secure housing, adequate income and a settled home life. Just as importantly, they tend to become parents through deliberate choice rather than circumstance, which often means they approach the role with greater commitment and emotional maturity.

Later parenthood has also changed opportunities for women in particular. When childbearing no longer coincides with the years in which careers are established, women are far better able to gain qualifications and seniority before taking time away from work. This not only benefits individual families financially but also allows economies to make fuller use of the skills of half their population.

That said, the drawbacks are not trivial. Fertility declines with age, and some couples who delay discover that conceiving is difficult or impossible, often after considerable emotional and financial strain. At a societal level, later parenthood tends to lower birth rates, compounding the challenges of an ageing population. Yet these concerns are arguably better addressed by making earlier parenthood more feasible, through affordable childcare and housing, than by regarding the choice to wait as a problem in itself.

In conclusion, while delaying parenthood can bring biological and demographic costs, the greater stability it affords children and the wider opportunities it creates for parents, especially mothers, outweigh them. I therefore regard this trend as largely positive.
